title: NVIDIA changes leadership and pledges continuity
lead: NVIDIA confirmed chief executive Jensen Huang’s resignation; finance chief Colette Kress became interim leader. The board says operations, customer commitments and product plans will continue.

news.title: NVIDIA changes leadership while pledging to maintain its product plans
news.summary: NVIDIA confirmed chief executive Jensen Huang’s resignation and finance chief Colette Kress’s interim appointment. For robot developers, this changes governance at a computing supplier; it does not establish that its products have stopped.
news.details: On November 12, NVIDIA announced Jensen Huang's departure as president, chief executive and board member. Colette Kress became interim chief executive while retaining her chief financial officer duties; a permanent successor is still being sought. NVIDIA's filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission says the board accepted the resignation on November 11. That is the decision date, whereas November 12 is the public announcement date. The leadership change at a supplier of AI computing equipment is a confirmed event, rather than an inference from reports about the scandal.
news.technical_novelty: NVIDIA confirmed chief executive Jensen Huang’s resignation and finance chief Colette Kress’s interim appointment. For robot developers, this changes governance at a computing supplier; it does not establish that its products have stopped. The crisis surrounding Huang has a separate investigative process: on November 10, independent directors said they had engaged outside lawyers to investigate. TechCrunch describes the controversy as arising from reported extramarital relationships and scrutiny of China-related chip sales. TechCrunch and Reuters independently reported the resignation, but reports of possible misconduct are not findings of that investigation. The cited official documents do not publish such findings. NVIDIA's board says operations, customer commitments and product plans should continue without interruption. That is the company's position about future operations; it does not independently establish that customers will see no disruption. Financial results and the accompanying investor call remain scheduled for November 17.
news.engineering_impact: NVIDIA confirmed chief executive Jensen Huang’s resignation and finance chief Colette Kress’s interim appointment. For robot developers, this changes governance at a computing supplier; it does not establish that its products have stopped. The next specific disclosure point named by NVIDIA is its November 17 financial report and management discussion. Resignation alone establishes neither a broken roadmap nor guaranteed unchanged developer terms: the disclosed event is a governance transition, not a specification revision.
news.limitations: NVIDIA confirmed chief executive Jensen Huang’s resignation and finance chief Colette Kress’s interim appointment. For robot developers, this changes governance at a computing supplier; it does not establish that its products have stopped. The next specific disclosure point named by NVIDIA is its November 17 financial report and management discussion. Resignation alone establishes neither a broken roadmap nor guaranteed unchanged developer terms: the disclosed event is a governance transition, not a specification revision.
news.evidence_status: Leadership change is confirmed by the official release and U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing; an investigation and reported allegations are not findings of guilt.
news.body:
On November 12, NVIDIA announced Jensen Huang's departure as president, chief executive and board member. Colette Kress became interim chief executive while retaining her chief financial officer duties; a permanent successor is still being sought. NVIDIA's filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission says the board accepted the resignation on November 11. That is the decision date, whereas November 12 is the public announcement date. The leadership change at a supplier of AI computing equipment is a confirmed event, rather than an inference from reports about the scandal.

The crisis surrounding Huang has a separate investigative process: on November 10, independent directors said they had engaged outside lawyers to investigate. TechCrunch describes the controversy as arising from reported extramarital relationships and scrutiny of China-related chip sales. TechCrunch and Reuters independently reported the resignation, but reports of possible misconduct are not findings of that investigation. The cited official documents do not publish such findings. NVIDIA's board says operations, customer commitments and product plans should continue without interruption. That is the company's position about future operations; it does not independently establish that customers will see no disruption. Financial results and the accompanying investor call remain scheduled for November 17.

A team relying on NVIDIA computing should distinguish corporate risk from the condition of a particular tool. The leadership announcement does not cancel shipments, end support or change software compatibility. Equally, the board's commitment to continuity does not replace documentation for the actual hardware and software versions used in a robot.

The next specific disclosure point named by NVIDIA is its November 17 financial report and management discussion. Resignation alone establishes neither a broken roadmap nor guaranteed unchanged developer terms: the disclosed event is a governance transition, not a specification revision.

news.title: ASUS splits packing-robot control into four layers
news.summary: ASUS described a two-arm robot packing accessories at a group factory. Its 99.5%-within-20-seconds target is not presented as an already achieved result.
news.details: On November 13, ASUS described Gallop, its robot program for factory workstations. Today it is a fixed-base, two-arm system learning to pack accessories for motherboards, the main circuit boards connecting a computer’s components, at an ASUS group plant. The station contains 15 small parts, many in thin transparent bags. ASUS sets a target of 99.5% success while completing a kit within 20 seconds. In the article, that is the required standard, not a published measurement of reliability already achieved. A wheeled version, customer pilots in 2027 and market availability in the second half of 2028 remain plans.
news.technical_novelty: ASUS described a two-arm robot packing accessories at a group factory. Its 99.5%-within-20-seconds target is not presented as an already achieved result. ASUS describes four control layers: planning steps, separately checking their execution, reaching and grasping skills, and precise arm control. Fixed interfaces — agreed rules for exchanging data — connect them so that models can change without rebuilding the whole robot. An onboard NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor computer runs the system. Training uses recordings of consenting workers, variations in computer-simulated conditions and demonstrations guided by a person wearing a headset and gloves. ASUS still plans to integrate its own touch-sensitive hand. The intended design should therefore not be mistaken for the exact configuration already operating on the current rig.
news.engineering_impact: ASUS described a two-arm robot packing accessories at a group factory. Its 99.5%-within-20-seconds target is not presented as an already achieved result. Fixed interfaces can make model replacement easier at the design level, but do not themselves establish preserved latency or quality after a swap. The description supplies no such comparison. Both the touch-sensitive hand and wheeled base still belong to the announced development sequence rather than a single fully demonstrated configuration.

Fixed interfaces can make model replacement easier at the design level, but do not themselves establish preserved latency or quality after a swap. The description supplies no such comparison. Both the touch-sensitive hand and wheeled base still belong to the announced development sequence rather than a single fully demonstrated configuration.
news.evidence_status: Developer announcement; stated plans and capabilities are not an independent test.
news.body:
On November 13, ASUS described Gallop, its robot program for factory workstations. Today it is a fixed-base, two-arm system learning to pack accessories for motherboards, the main circuit boards connecting a computer’s components, at an ASUS group plant. The station contains 15 small parts, many in thin transparent bags. ASUS sets a target of 99.5% success while completing a kit within 20 seconds. In the article, that is the required standard, not a published measurement of reliability already achieved. A wheeled version, customer pilots in 2027 and market availability in the second half of 2028 remain plans.

ASUS describes four control layers: planning steps, separately checking their execution, reaching and grasping skills, and precise arm control. Fixed interfaces — agreed rules for exchanging data — connect them so that models can change without rebuilding the whole robot. An onboard NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor computer runs the system. Training uses recordings of consenting workers, variations in computer-simulated conditions and demonstrations guided by a person wearing a headset and gloves. ASUS still plans to integrate its own touch-sensitive hand. The intended design should therefore not be mistaken for the exact configuration already operating on the current rig.

A distinct execution-checking layer is architecturally significant: generating a sequence and establishing that a step actually finished are different functions. ASUS assigns them to separate layers. Without a published protocol, however, it remains unclear which observations confirm completion and how the system distinguishes a failed grasp from a successfully transferred part.

Fixed interfaces can make model replacement easier at the design level, but do not themselves establish preserved latency or quality after a swap. The description supplies no such comparison. Both the touch-sensitive hand and wheeled base still belong to the announced development sequence rather than a single fully demonstrated configuration.

news.title: Gaze context can clarify a request without completing it
news.summary: A team including Tsinghua University introduced HEIR, a collection of speech, gaze and robot-motion records for household assistance. In a separate integrated autonomous test, the system completed 18.52% of 27 requests.
news.details: A team including Tsinghua University posted a research preprint on November 12 about grounding household robot requests in speech, measured gaze and video from the person's viewpoint. Its HEIR dataset pairs those signals with robot observations and recorded movements. An operator controlled the robot during data collection: these are demonstrations, not thousands of independently completed requests. Seventeen participants contributed 300 sessions totaling 38.56 hours. The evaluation covers identifying the intended object, planning steps, moving around and manipulating objects with the arms.
news.technical_novelty: A team including Tsinghua University introduced HEIR, a collection of speech, gaze and robot-motion records for household assistance. In a separate integrated autonomous test, the system completed 18.52% of 27 requests. The Tsinghua team’s system first interprets a request, then uses the current state to decide whether to continue a step, switch to the next one or finish. The authors compared models on recordings and ran separate autonomous experiments on a physical robot. The integrated system completed 18.52% of 27 evaluated requests. Better scores for individual actions do not establish equal reliability for the whole assistant. Gaze contributions were isolated mainly through controlled comparisons on recorded data; live sessions diverge in human behavior and object arrangement. The result does not establish dependable assistance in an arbitrary home or for a person outside the tested setting.
news.engineering_impact: A team including Tsinghua University introduced HEIR, a collection of speech, gaze and robot-motion records for household assistance. In a separate integrated autonomous test, the system completed 18.52% of 27 requests. The paper isolates gaze contributions through controlled comparisons on recordings. Whole-robot success also depends on request interpretation, transitions between steps, navigation and grasping. The 18.52% result is therefore neither an isolated score for gaze sensing nor evidence that the assistant is ready for arbitrary homes.

In a separate integrated autonomous test, the system completed 18.52% of 27 requests. The paper isolates gaze contributions through controlled comparisons on recordings. Whole-robot success also depends on request interpretation, transitions between steps, navigation and grasping. The 18.52% result is therefore neither an isolated score for gaze sensing nor evidence that the assistant is ready for arbitrary homes.
news.evidence_status: Preprint and author-run experiments; independent reproduction is not confirmed.
news.organization: Tsinghua University; Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence; Fudan University; Yangu Robotics
news.body:
A team including Tsinghua University posted a research preprint on November 12 about grounding household robot requests in speech, measured gaze and video from the person's viewpoint. Its HEIR dataset pairs those signals with robot observations and recorded movements. An operator controlled the robot during data collection: these are demonstrations, not thousands of independently completed requests. Seventeen participants contributed 300 sessions totaling 38.56 hours. The evaluation covers identifying the intended object, planning steps, moving around and manipulating objects with the arms.

The Tsinghua team’s system first interprets a request, then uses the current state to decide whether to continue a step, switch to the next one or finish. The authors compared models on recordings and ran separate autonomous experiments on a physical robot. The integrated system completed 18.52% of 27 evaluated requests. Better scores for individual actions do not establish equal reliability for the whole assistant. Gaze contributions were isolated mainly through controlled comparisons on recorded data; live sessions diverge in human behavior and object arrangement. The result does not establish dependable assistance in an arbitrary home or for a person outside the tested setting.

Reproduction requires preserving the boundaries between three forms of evidence. Collection trajectories were controlled by a person; offline model comparisons score individual predictions; physical end-to-end tests check actual request completion. Neither training-set size nor next-action accuracy is a count of autonomously completed household jobs, and those measures answer different experimental questions.

The paper isolates gaze contributions through controlled comparisons on recordings. Whole-robot success also depends on request interpretation, transitions between steps, navigation and grasping. The 18.52% result is therefore neither an isolated score for gaze sensing nor evidence that the assistant is ready for arbitrary homes.

news.title: GXO ties wider Apollo trials to warehouse operating measures
news.summary: GXO and Apptronik plan expanded warehouse trials from 2027. A potential rollout of up to 1,000 humanoids depends on agreed requirements, rather than a demonstrated robot movement alone.
news.details: Logistics company GXO and robot developer Apptronik announced a letter of intent on November 12 to expand warehouse trials of the human-shaped Apollo robot. Tests in live operations are planned from 2027, covering picking, case and tote movement, packing and sorting. The proposed scale is up to 1,000 robots over four years, explicitly conditional on meeting agreed productivity, safety and operational measures. Initial commercial deployment in North America is intended for late 2027. This is a conditional expansion plan, not an announcement that a thousand machines have been delivered.
news.technical_novelty: GXO and Apptronik plan expanded warehouse trials from 2027. A potential rollout of up to 1,000 humanoids depends on agreed requirements, rather than a demonstrated robot movement alone. GXO and Apptronik envisage a service model: robot use would be provided as a service that can expand as applications become ready. Prices, maintenance coverage and the allocation of individual costs are not disclosed. GXO reports an earlier pilot for picking small consumer goods and evaluations of more than 50 logistics tasks at Apptronik's training facility. That facility is not fifty customer warehouses. Independent Forbes coverage highlights an economic limitation: GXO's chief executive had previously said humanoid investment had not yet paid off. The agreement itself provides no payback calculation for the future program.
news.engineering_impact: GXO and Apptronik plan expanded warehouse trials from 2027. A potential rollout of up to 1,000 humanoids depends on agreed requirements, rather than a demonstrated robot movement alone. Numerical acceptance thresholds for individual applications are not published. Without allowed intervention counts or recovery-time requirements, the thousand-unit ceiling describes intended scale rather than a reproducible level of operational readiness. Those missing measures determine what the planned trials actually have to establish.
news.limitations: GXO and Apptronik plan expanded warehouse trials from 2027. A potential rollout of up to 1,000 humanoids depends on agreed requirements, rather than a demonstrated robot movement alone. Numerical acceptance thresholds for individual applications are not published. Without allowed intervention counts or recovery-time requirements, the thousand-unit ceiling describes intended scale rather than a reproducible level of operational readiness. Those missing measures determine what the planned trials actually have to establish.
news.evidence_status: Developer announcement; stated plans and capabilities are not an independent test.
news.body:
Logistics company GXO and robot developer Apptronik announced a letter of intent on November 12 to expand warehouse trials of the human-shaped Apollo robot. Tests in live operations are planned from 2027, covering picking, case and tote movement, packing and sorting. The proposed scale is up to 1,000 robots over four years, explicitly conditional on meeting agreed productivity, safety and operational measures. Initial commercial deployment in North America is intended for late 2027. This is a conditional expansion plan, not an announcement that a thousand machines have been delivered.

GXO and Apptronik envisage a service model: robot use would be provided as a service that can expand as applications become ready. Prices, maintenance coverage and the allocation of individual costs are not disclosed. GXO reports an earlier pilot for picking small consumer goods and evaluations of more than 50 logistics tasks at Apptronik's training facility. That facility is not fifty customer warehouses. Independent Forbes coverage highlights an economic limitation: GXO's chief executive had previously said humanoid investment had not yet paid off. The agreement itself provides no payback calculation for the future program.

The engineering task is to validate integration into live warehouse processes, not one successful grasp. Evaluation includes safety, security and technical requirements. The partners also intend to test operation alongside existing automation and people, so an isolated demonstration score cannot substitute for evidence from the intended picking or transport workflow.

Numerical acceptance thresholds for individual applications are not published. Without allowed intervention counts or recovery-time requirements, the thousand-unit ceiling describes intended scale rather than a reproducible level of operational readiness. Those missing measures determine what the planned trials actually have to establish.

news.title: Autoware is being adapted for a full-size Munich city bus
news.summary: TIER IV and the Technical University of Munich described responsibilities for automated bus driving. Route operation is planned after controlled tests and with personnel aboard for safety.
news.details: Japan's TIER IV and the Technical University of Munich announced support on November 11 for automated-driving development on a full-size city bus in Munich. The basis is Autoware, automated-driving software whose development TIER IV leads. Its source code is available for study and modification. The bus still needs adaptation to local roads and testing. Bus manufacturer MAN is responsible for vehicle-control mechanisms and low-level software; the university handles sensor configuration and the driving system. After tests in controlled conditions, the partners plan operation on existing routes with personnel aboard to ensure safety.
news.technical_novelty: TIER IV and the Technical University of Munich described responsibilities for automated bus driving. Route operation is planned after controlled tests and with personnel aboard for safety. The effort uses a joint research center established in October. It draws on experience deploying the Autoware automated-driving software in Japanese buses, but does not simply install unchanged software on another vehicle: both the vehicle platform and road conditions differ. A university professor describes federal support of 20 million euros over three years for the Munich bus-development project. That is project-wide funding, not an announced budget solely for Autoware software. The release supplies no Munich route-trial results, measured reduction in crashes or promise to remove the onboard safety personnel at the outset.
news.engineering_impact: TIER IV and the Technical University of Munich described responsibilities for automated bus driving. Route operation is planned after controlled tests and with personnel aboard for safety. The intended route stage includes onboard safety personnel. Future test comparisons will therefore need their authority and intervention conditions, alongside the vehicle configuration. Describing the software platform without those operating conditions would not establish whether two bus projects demonstrate the same degree of independent driving.
news.limitations: TIER IV and the Technical University of Munich described responsibilities for automated bus driving. Route operation is planned after controlled tests and with personnel aboard for safety. The intended route stage includes onboard safety personnel. Future test comparisons will therefore need their authority and intervention conditions, alongside the vehicle configuration. Describing the software platform without those operating conditions would not establish whether two bus projects demonstrate the same degree of independent driving.

news.organization: TIER IV; Technical University of Munich; MAN
news.body:
Japan's TIER IV and the Technical University of Munich announced support on November 11 for automated-driving development on a full-size city bus in Munich. The basis is Autoware, automated-driving software whose development TIER IV leads. Its source code is available for study and modification. The bus still needs adaptation to local roads and testing. Bus manufacturer MAN is responsible for vehicle-control mechanisms and low-level software; the university handles sensor configuration and the driving system. After tests in controlled conditions, the partners plan operation on existing routes with personnel aboard to ensure safety.

The effort uses a joint research center established in October. It draws on experience deploying the Autoware automated-driving software in Japanese buses, but does not simply install unchanged software on another vehicle: both the vehicle platform and road conditions differ. A university professor describes federal support of 20 million euros over three years for the Munich bus-development project. That is project-wide funding, not an announced budget solely for Autoware software. The release supplies no Munich route-trial results, measured reduction in crashes or promise to remove the onboard safety personnel at the outset.

The division of work identifies the limits of a portable software solution. Driving depends on sensors, vehicle actuators and road conditions as well as algorithms. MAN's vehicle-control work and the university's sensor configuration imply a separate integration effort, rather than automatic compatibility between every bus and an unchanged software installation.

The intended route stage includes onboard safety personnel. Future test comparisons will therefore need their authority and intervention conditions, alongside the vehicle configuration. Describing the software platform without those operating conditions would not establish whether two bus projects demonstrate the same degree of independent driving.
